title: "Inspect what your beliefs imply"
output: rmarkdown::html_document

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 144
)
library(suppose)
```

Two intervals can look reasonable on their own and imply quite different
answers to the question you care about. Here we investigate an invented claim:
higher cure temperature increases mean strength by more than 5 MPa.

## Distinguish means from measurements

The tutorial judgments assign 90% probability to the **population mean** falling
between 45–55 MPa at 140 °C and 51–65 MPa at 160 °C. They are not prediction
intervals for individual batches. Known batch SDs of 3 MPa supply a separate
measurement-variation assumption.

```{r model}
record <- suppose_example()
independent <- record$revisions[[2]]$candidate
correlated <- record$revisions[[3]]$candidate
```

```{r marginals, fig.alt="Normal prior densities for mean strength at 140 and 160 degrees Celsius, centered at 50 and 58 MPa respectively."}
plot_prior(correlated, view = "means")
```

`fit_prior()` fits normal quantiles by least squares and reports elicited versus
implied quantiles. Quantiles that the method cannot represent adequately prevent
numerical acceptance. Plausible ranges with no probability interpretation remain
unfitted judgments.

## Ask which assumptions matter

The first candidate assumes independent mean uncertainty. The second keeps the
same marginal judgments but sets their correlation to 0.8. Neither correlation
can be learned from the two marginal intervals.

```{r compare}
probability <- function(prior) {
  predict_prior(prior, seed = 47)$summary$mean_difference$probability_above
}
data.frame(
  correlation = c(0, 0.8),
  probability_gain_above_5 = round(
    c(probability(independent), probability(correlated)),
    3
  )
)
```

Positive correlation makes the two uncertain means move together, reducing
uncertainty in their difference. The probability changes even though neither
marginal interval has changed. This is a consequence of an assumption, not new
evidence for the claim.

```{r differences, fig.alt="Prior distributions of the mean strength contrast and a future-batch contrast, with a reference at a 5 MPa gain."}
plot_prior(correlated, view = "contrast")
```

## Keep additional expectations visible

An answer can be worth keeping even when it cannot be fitted.

```{r expectation}
comparison <- judgment(
  160,
  kind = "comparison",
  reference_condition = 140,
  units = "MPa",
  author = "Tutorial researcher",
  answer = "I expect a higher mean at 160, but have not stated a probability."
)
record <- record_judgment(record, comparison, "Retain a qualitative comparison")
```

Ranges, explicit quantiles, comparisons, and shape judgments retain their
original wording and interpretation. A straight-line projection beyond the two
anchors is available only with an additional, explicit assumption:

```{r projection}
checks <- check_expectations(record, linear = TRUE)
```

This does not make a line a consequence of the original judgments. A peak or
other incompatible shape remains a limitation to investigate. See
`check_expectations()` for the returned comparisons and unsupported checks.

## Review before accepting

`accept_revision()` records who reviewed a numerical candidate, why it expresses
the intended judgment, and what evidence could challenge it. The previous
candidate remains available. Editing the meaning does not silently transfer
acceptance to a different model.

For the mathematics and support restrictions, see [methods and limits](methods.html).

and prior exposure.
